rv.q: So much goes right in this exceptional production that it's quite simply a killer Mockingbird.

This much will be familiar to fans of Harper Lee’s 1960 novel, one of the most beloved in all literature, and the classic 1962 film starring Gregory Peck. But this adaptation, written by The West Wing’s Aaron Sorkin and directed by Bartlett Sher, has set box-office records in America and has new dialogue as well as a new spin.
Sheer emotion and moral force make this Broadway adaptation of Harper Lee’s novel about race, community and family a powerfully uplifting theatrical event.
Aaron Sorkin finds effective ways in his confident adaptation, drawing out the lawyer’s moral inconsistencies without undermining his goodness completely.
Otherwise, this is a tremendously effective adaptation that not only does justice to the original but, where it matters most, improves upon it.
Throw in a doddery but decent judge (Jim Norton) and a terrified Mayella (Poppy Lee Friar) and you have a seriously satisfying, satisfyingly serious evening.

Hats off to Aaron Sorkin. While the official title may be Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, this captivating drama is very much Sorkin's take on a story that has become embedded in the consciousness of generations of readers.
Breathing fresh life into one of the most famous characters of all time is no small achievement.
There is a lot of talking, shifting of vast clumps of set, period costumes, but not enough theatrical imagination on display in either the staging or the script.
Nevertheless, this is a thin, often awkward evening.
Spall handles moral outrage with an understated command that invites empathy for this man on all fronts.
Together, the two men have fashioned a stage version of Harper Lee’s 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird, finally here at the Gielgud from Broadway, that is as entertaining as it is ambitiously lofty.
That’s an odd failing for a play about ethics.
Aaron Sorkin’s To Kill a Mockingbird is powerful, moving, and brimming with humour; a magnificently awe-inspiring piece of theatre.
A phenomenal production, A Mockingbird really is worthy of all the hype and definitely worth the extensive wait.

cn.t: Sorkin's adaptation wins widespread praise for its razor-sharp dialogue and powerful relevance, with Rafe Spall's Atticus earning acclaim. A few critics find it overly polished and lacking atmosphere, but most call it spellbinding theater.
